title: Optically Derived Radio-Frequency Benchmark in Methanol: A Sub-kHz Reference for Astrophysical Tests of Fundamental Physics
authors: Frank M. J. Cozijn, Arthémise Altman, Alexandr S. Bogomolov, Alexis Libert, Simon Collignon, Erik Dierikx, Jeroen C. J. Koelemeij, Boy Lankhaar, Isabelle Kleiner, Clément Lauzin, Wim Ubachs
abstract: Methanol radio lines observed in space provide sensitive probes of whether the proton-to-electron mass ratio has changed over cosmic time, but such tests require laboratory rest frequencies with very high accuracy. Here we determine the frequency of the astrophysically important 12.2 GHz $3_{-1}$E -- $2_{0}$E transition of CH$_3$OH by measuring near-infrared rovibrational transitions rather than the microwave line directly. Using wavelength-modulated NICE-OHMS locked to an ultra-stable optical frequency comb and referenced via a fiber link to a hydrogen-maser frequency standard, we measure Lamb-dip frequencies near 1.4 $μ$m (216 THz) with 10 Hz statistical reproducibility and absolute uncertainties as low as 130 Hz. Pairs of optical transitions sharing common upper levels form a triangulation scheme that yields the ground-state rotational combination difference. We obtain 12 178 596.415(135) kHz, improving on earlier molecular-beam microwave spectroscopy by a factor of 20 and agreeing with a recent free-induction-decay measurement. This result establishes a sub-kHz laboratory benchmark for a key radio-astronomical methanol line and demonstrates that optical triangulation can be extended to non-chiral molecules with internal rotation.
summary: The authors report establishing an unprecedentedly precise laboratory benchmark for the methanol radio line used in astrophysics. They achieve this by measuring related near-infrared optical transitions and combining them via a quantum 'triangulation' method, bypassing direct microwave measurement limitations. This high accuracy significantly enhances the potential of molecular spectroscopy to test fundamental physical constants over cosmic timescales.
main_problem: The goal is to determine a highly accurate laboratory rest frequency for the astrophysically important 12.2 GHz methanol transition to enable precise tests of fundamental physics, such as variations in the proton-to-electron mass ratio.
main_result: A sub-kHz benchmark frequency was established for this key radio line with an uncertainty of $135 	ext{ Hz}$, representing a 20-fold improvement over previous microwave spectroscopy methods.
method: The measurement avoids direct microwave observation by using a novel optical 'triangulation scheme' involving pairs of near-infrared rovibrational transitions, which are then combined to yield the ground-state rotational difference frequency.
model_or_system: The system is methanol ($	ext{CH}_3	ext{OH}$), treated as an achiral asymmetric rotor exhibiting hindered internal rotation. The symmetry analysis uses the Longuet–Higgins group $G_6$, which allows for a closed electric-dipole transition loop that would otherwise be forbidden by simple parity rules.
key_observables: The derived frequency of the $3_{-1}^E - 20^E$ rotational combination difference, measured via near-infrared Lamb-dip frequencies ($\approx 1.4 \mu	ext{m}$).
important_parameters: Statistical reproducibility of $10 	ext{ Hz}$ and absolute uncertainties as low as $130 	ext{ Hz}$. The measurement relies on locking to an ultra-stable optical frequency comb referenced to a hydrogen maser.
main_assumptions: The systematic error from unresolved hyperfine structure is estimated at $\approx 10 	ext{ Hz}$, and the underlying multiplet is assumed to blend into a single symmetric profile.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the quantum level scheme used for the triangulation, connecting three common upper levels. Other figures detail the experimental setup using NICE-OHMS and frequency stability comparisons against external standards.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical necessity (testing fundamental constants), outlines the advanced spectroscopic technique (optical triangulation on $	ext{CH}_3	ext{OH}$), describes the high-precision measurement platform (NICE-OHMS locked to an OFC/H-maser), and finally presents the derived, highly accurate frequency benchmark.
why_interesting: This work exemplifies how advanced molecular spectroscopy techniques—specifically using optical transitions to deduce microwave frequencies—can push precision limits far beyond what is achievable by direct measurement. The theoretical underpinning involving symmetry breaking due to internal rotation is a rich topic in molecular physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Partial quantum level scheme of CH3OH. Rotational states are indicated within colored boxes representing the vi- brational ground (red) and excited (blue, green) levels. The green color-coded rotational levels pertain to the same excited vibration, whereas the blue color-coded rotational level refers to another excited vibration. The six target transitions ∆i,j (indicated with frequencies in cm−1 units as obtained from the lower-resolution study [30]) form a triangulation scheme connecting three common upper levels (i = 1, 2, 3) to the 3−1E (j = 1) and 20E (j = 2) ground states to determine the splitting ∆i.

FIG. 4. Frequency comparison of the in-house Cs-clock against the VSL Hydrogen maser, obtained by counting the Cs-clock 10 MHz signal against the H-maser over the TFN. The data (smoothed by a 10,000-second moving average) re- veals fractional frequency deviations of ±1×10−12 and a sys- tematic offset from UTC(VSL) (orange dashed line). Typ- ically, UTC(VSL) drifts by less than 1 ns/day relative to UTC, corresponding to a negligible fractional frequency offset of ≲1 × 10−14. The filtered time-domain data clearly illus- trates the slow frequency wander, characteristic of flicker and random-walk noise, inherent to the free-running Cs-clock.
